original_question: Let G be a finitely generated residually finite group with residual finiteness growth function F_S^G(n) = max{D(g) : |g|_S <= n}, where D(g) is the minimum index of a finite-index normal subgroup of G that does not contain the nontrivial element g. Does there exist such a group whose residual finiteness growth is intermediate, meaning that F_S^G grows faster than every polynomial function but slower than every exponential function?
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s actual target. It correctly identifies the setting of finitely generated residually finite groups, the depth D(g), the residual finiteness growth function F^G_S, and the precise existence question about whether this growth can be intermediate, i.e. superpolynomial but subexponential. This is exactly the open problem stated in the paper as Question 1.3.
missing_details: The paper states the problem as an existence question for a finitely generated residually finite group G, with the generating set S understood as part of the definition of F^G_S.
To make the question fully stand-alone, |g|_S should be identified as word length with respect to the finite generating set S.
Since D(g) is only defined for nontrivial elements in the surrounding discussion, the maximum in F^G_S(n) should be taken over nontrivial g, or this should be stated explicitly.

The paper emphasizes that F^G_S depends on the finite generating set only up to the usual equivalence of growth functions, so 'intermediate residual finiteness growth' is a property of G rather than of a particular choice of S.
The official formulation in the paper is narrower and cleaner than the draft: it does not ask for any broader classification, only for the existence of one such group.

The nearby context explains that this question is about the poorly understood 'slow' end of the spectrum, after Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.2 show that arbitrarily fast and many sufficiently fast residual finiteness growth types can occur.
refined_question: Does there exist a finitely generated residually finite group G such that, for one (equivalently any) finite generating set S, its residual finiteness growth function F^G_S(n), defined by F^G_S(n) = max{D_G(g) : g is nontrivial and |g|_S <= n}, where D_G(g) is the least index of a finite-index normal subgroup of G that does not contain g, has intermediate growth; that is, is superpolynomial but subexponential?
justification: The draft is aiming directly at the paper’s Question 1.3 in Section 1. The surrounding text first defines residual finiteness, depth, and the residual finiteness growth function, and notes that its growth type is independent of the choice of finite generating set up to the usual equivalence. Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 immediately before Question 1.3 explain why the unresolved issue is the existence of groups with genuinely intermediate residual finiteness growth, so the refined question should stay focused on that exact existence problem and not broaden into classification or variant notions.
